newsitem.title: UK: Mark creeps higher on its European cross rates.
newsitem.headline: Mark creeps higher on its European cross rates.

text.p: The mark was firmer on its European cross rates by midsession on Friday, encouraged by the dollar's inability to retake the 1.80-mark level, talk of central bank purchases and signs of an improving German economy.

The advent of the French government's public accounts audit early Monday has also kept traders wary of extending short-mark positions for fear the data may fuel some new doubts about the probability of European monetary union starting on time.
Analysts said the weak mark story may be wearing thin. There is little fresh news to keep up the momentum of mark selling and many technical targets have already been satisfied, they said.

"I think there's a natural resistance for the dollar around the psychological 1.80 (marks) that people are reluctant to test, we've come a long way with the mark and there is also a lot of interest in the French report Monday," said Peter Wood, trader at the Bank of Boston.

Confirmation about a steady improvement in the German economy, meantime, was seen in the release of the June business activity index from Germany's Ifo research institute. This was broadly in line with expectations, analysts said.
Traders were also wary of holding short-mark positions today as the European Union's monetary committee gathered today.

While officials have denied rumours that a revaluation of the punt is on the agenda, there is speculation that EMU conversion rates are up for discussion and talk that individual countries will have an interest to prevent further mark losses.
Dealers said the Bank of Italy was buying marks for lire on a number of occasions this week, while they said there was a strong suspicion the Bank of Spain was doing likewise for pesetas.
"Volumes have thinned out quite a bit for the summer at this stage and the market is certainly net short of marks," said Henry Wilkes, senior trader at Bank Julius Baer.
"Everyone seems a bit edgy up at these levels and longer term asset players are viewing the mark as pretty good value against currencies like sterling," said Wilkes.

Analysts said there is also some suspicion Asian central banks looking to rebase their reserve portfolios ahead of European monetary union may also be keen to pick up marks at multi-year lows, effectively picking up "cheap" euros.

Traders said concerns about the Bundesbank nudging up German market rates in the months ahead is also still lingering, with comments from Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler today linking surging stock markets with money supply concerns.
Elsewhere, the overwhelmingly mark negative bias amongst analysts in recently has also started to turn this week.

In notes issued to clients this week, analysts at JP Morgan said mark weakness in the European exchange rate mechanism was over and analysts at Goldman Sachs said the market is now close to "great levels" to buy the mark against sterling, dollar and Swiss franc.
At 1150 GMT, the mark was trading at 973.20/50 lire compared with 972.30/60 late Thursday. Mark/peseta was at 84.26/28 versus 84.23/25 yesterday. Mark/Paris was 3.3780/85 versus 3.3785/90.
